aiAgentFacts.fact: In a blinded nested case-control study of 57 cats, those with early owner-reported mobility changes scored significantly lower on the Feline Musculoskeletal Pain Index (P=0.003) than control cats.
Case cats had significantly higher total pain scores (P<0.0001), crepitus (P=0.002) and joint thickening (P=0.003) on orthopaedic examination.
Presence of bilateral disease was significantly more likely in case cats (P=0.005, OR 14), as was the number of bilaterally affected joints (P=0.001).
The groups did not differ significantly in age category, breed, sex, temperament or body condition score, so the findings are not explained by case cats simply being older or heavier.
Of the VetMetrica quality-of-life domains, only Comfort differentiated the groups (P=0.002); Vitality and Emotional Wellbeing were reported as not significant.
The authors concluded that recognising mobility impairment earlier would allow interventions aimed at slowing disease progression — a stated rationale, not an outcome this study tested.
The inference runs from owner observation to examination findings; the study does not establish what proportion of cats with joint disease have owners who notice.
Total sample was 57 cats (30 case, 27 control); effect sizes such as the OR of 14 carry wide uncertainty at this scale.

historyQuestions: Supported by the study's inclusion criterion rather than prescribed by it: early owner-reported mobility change was itself the case-defining variable, and it separated groups that examination then confirmed differed — which supports asking about mobility change directly rather than waiting for lameness.
redFlags: Not addressed — this study identifies no red-flag findings and defines no urgency threshold.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the study contrasts cats with and without owner-reported mobility change and does not evaluate other causes of reduced mobility.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: The study's own measures: the Feline Musculoskeletal Pain Index completed by the owner, plus a hands-on orthopaedic examination scoring pain, crepitus, thickening and bilateral involvement.

limitations: Small sample: 57 cats total (30 case, 27 control), so effect estimates including the OR of 14 for bilateral disease carry wide uncertainty
Recruitment favoured engaged owners willing to accept a home visit and two weeks of accelerometer wear; the informativeness of their observations may not generalise to less attentive owners
Inference direction is observation to examination — the study cannot estimate how often joint disease goes unnoticed by owners

The abstract reports Vitality (P=0.009) and Emotional Wellbeing (P=0.018) as non-significant without stating the significance threshold; correction for multiple comparisons is a plausible explanation but is not stated by the paper
No accelerometry result is reported in the abstract despite two weeks of collection, so the objective activity measure's contribution is unknown
Orthopaedic examination scoring involves subjective clinical judgement; blinding mitigates but does not eliminate this
Cross-sectional: no follow-up establishes whether earlier recognition changes outcome, despite that being the authors' stated motivation
